analysis.one_liner: Locks in the weaker 2008 mining stream buffer rule and blocks stricter stream protections for five years.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 229-192 in March 2014, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a December 2008 rule on stream buffers and mining waste into every state's coal mining program, effectively making it the permanent national standard. It then bars the Interior Department from issuing any new rules on stream buffer zones or stream protection until it finishes a five-year study and reports to Congress. The upshot is that the weaker 2008 standards stay in place for years, and any replacement rule is put off at least that long.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies gain the most: the 2008 rule allows excess spoil and mine waste to be placed closer to streams than the older 1983 buffer standard did, and the bill would lock that in while blocking the Interior Department's work on a stricter replacement. Mining states that want to run their own programs also gain certainty, and the industry argues the current rules protect mining jobs. Consumers of coal-fired electricity could see marginally lower costs if production constraints stay loose.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state with an approved surface coal mining program to adopt the December 2008 Office of Surface Mining rule on excess spoil, coal mine waste, and stream buffers within two years.
Declares the 2008 rule to be compliant with the Endangered Species Act based on 2006-2007 discussions with the Fish and Wildlife Service, shielding it from re-litigation on that ground.

Prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any regulations on stream buffer zones or stream protection until after a five-year implementation study and a report to Congress, other than rules needed to implement the 2008 rule itself.
Directs the study and report to evaluate ways the rule 'inhibits energy production,' framing the review toward identifying what to loosen rather than what to strengthen.

analysis.who_pays: People who live downstream of Appalachian surface mines — where excess rock and mine waste are placed in valleys and near headwater streams — would bear the cost in degraded water quality and buried streams for at least the study period. Taxpayers can also bear reclamation costs when mined land is not fully restored. Anyone who wanted a stronger national stream protection standard loses the ability to get one for years.

drawbacks.text: The bill freezes stream protection standards at the 2008 level and bars any new stream buffer or stream protection rule for the length of the five-year study plus report, delaying stronger safeguards indefinitely.

It binds every state mining program to a single decade-old federal rule written under a prior administration, rather than letting states or the federal agency update standards as science on mining's water impacts develops.
The required report is directed to evaluate 'any ways in which the existing rule inhibits energy production' — a one-way framing that asks what to relax, not whether protections should be stronger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry gets regulatory certainty and locked-in standards that let mining waste be placed near streams; the public gets no new stream protections for at least five years and a study rigged toward loosening. For a bill titled 'Preventing Government Waste,' it functions mainly as a multi-year moratorium on tighter rules, and the cost lands on the water quality of mining-adjacent communities.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House on a mostly party-line vote in March 2014, then sat on the Senate calendar for eight months without ever coming to a vote before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on a 24-15 vote in November 2013, and it was reported in February 2014.
On March 25, 2014 the House passed the bill 229-192, with 219 of 232 Republicans voting yes and 10 of 199 Democrats joining; seven Republicans voted no.

A Democratic motion to recommit — which would have clarified the bill does not limit hiring unemployed workers and veterans or using U.S.-made mining equipment — failed 197-224, with only 2 Republicans supporting it.
Amendments from Reps. Lowenthal and Cartwright were defeated during floor consideration under a rule that allowed only limited debate on those amendments.

The Senate received the bill on March 26, 2014, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders in May 2014 — where it remained with no committee action, no debate, and no vote through the end of the 113th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in the Senate without a vote, coal mining companies did not get the 2008 stream standards locked in or a five-year moratorium on stricter rules, and the Interior Department remained free to keep working on its own stream protection rulemaking. Communities living downstream of surface mines were spared the bill's delay of stronger safeguards.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 219 of 232 Republicans voted yes while 185 of 199 Democrats voted no; 10 Democrats crossed over to yes and 7 Republicans voted no.

industries.note: The bill locks the December 2008 stream buffer rule into every state program and blocks any stricter stream protection rule for at least the five-year study period, entrenching standards that permit placing mining waste near streams. The industry's gain in regulatory certainty comes at the cost of weaker water safeguards for communities downstream of mines.
With looser mining constraints in place, utilities could face fewer supply and cost pressures on coal. But the Senate never passed the bill, so no effect materialized.
States would have gotten a clear federal mandate to adopt the 2008 rule, preserving state-run programs under fixed federal terms rather than facing a shifting federal rule.
